To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the establishment of persistent infection and the development of oncogenic transformation are both associated with the production of defective interfering (DI) particles by hamster cells infected and transformed by equine herpesvus type 1 (EVH-1).

defective-interfering particle preparations of equid herpesviruses can mediate both the co-establishment and maintenance of persistent herpesvirus infection and the establishment of oncogenesis in permissive cells in culture.

the production of defective-interferring (DI) particles by persistently infected and transformed hamster embryo cells is a critical factor in the establishment of persistent infection and transformation by EHV-1.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of herpesvirus defective interfering (DI) particles and their role in persistent infection and oncogenically-transformed cell lines.
the development of an experimental model system to investigate the role of herpesvirus defective-interfering virus particles in persistent infection and oncogenesis.
the role of defective-interferinig (DI) particles in the establishment of persistent infections and the development of oncogenic transformation.

(i) the DI particles are not the sole cause of the transformed state; (ii) they may be involved in the establishment of persistent infection and in the maintenance of the transformed state, and (iii) the DI particle genome may be integrated into the genome of the host cell.
DI particles are involved in the establishment of persistent infection and in the establishment of oncogenesis.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
DI particle production is a common feature of herpesvirus persistence in cell culture and may be a factor in the establishment and maintenance of herpesvirus-induced tumours in vivo.
the EHV-1 DI particles are a necessary component in the establishment and maintenance of a persistently infected cell line and the production of a tumour.
the DI particles of EHV-1 may be involved in a number of biological processes, including oncogenesis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
DI particles may be important in the establishment and maintenance of persistent herpesvirus infection in vivo.
